prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new tests of fundamental physics and the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single prize part to Katori and Ye, and my configuration has not changed since round 1. I will give the scientific reasons again and then answer the chair's first question directly. The new principle is the magic wavelength. Choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock levels are equal, and neutral atoms can be held tightly, free of Doppler and recoil effects, without perturbing the transition. That is Katori's idea. It is what lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. Ye's work then showed that this statistical power can be combined with systematic control at the 10^-18 level, and he turned the lattice into a many-body system whose interactions have to be understood. A citation written around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 many-atom realisation is not a third clock prize. Hall and Hansch gave us the comb that counts optical cycles, and Wineland gave us control of single ions. Neither prize covers trapping a large ensemble of neutral atoms without shifting the line, and that is the step that moved clocks from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18. On maturity, the result has been reproduced at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, and fibre-linked comparisons between laboratories agree. The measurement of gravitational redshift over millimetres in a single sample is a delivered quantum-physics result, not a promise. It is a case where precision theory has to match experiment term by term. I also do not want to overstate the post-reading convergence. I came to this configuration on my own, and I rank it first for the reasons above, not because six of us now agree.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still novelty. A sceptic can say that the comb and ion-control prizes already recognised the foundations of optical clocks, and that this is excellent metrology and not a discovery about nature. I have no result to answer that with of the kind I would most like to cite, such as a measured drift of a constant or a dark-matter signal. The clocks have so far set limits. The second concern is credit. Katori and Ye are named by all eight of us, but Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg and others did much of the hands-on evaluation work. The ytterbium and aluminium-ion lineages are adjacent. I do not have verified documents for the early lattice-clock proposals, and I would welcome an expert review of them before the final vote. The third concern is timing relative to the redefinition of the second, which has not happened. I do not think the committee should wait for it, but I accept that others may.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is answered by the magic-wavelength concept and the many-atom statistical gain, which ion clocks cannot offer, and that the citation must be written carefully around the lattice and not around clocks or combs in general. He also argues that a prize recognises demonstrated performance and not the metrological decision on the second.
responses.response: I agree with both points and I have rewritten my citation along his lines. It now names the magic-wavelength lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, and it avoids general wording about atomic clocks or frequency standards. I would add one physical argument to his. In an ion clock the limit is the signal from one particle, so the statistics are poor. In a lattice clock the limit is the control of systematic shifts in a large ensemble. This is a different problem, and it brings in collisions, hyperfine-induced and higher-order light shifts that need careful theory. That is why I think the lattice clock is not simply an ion-clock refinement. On his second point I also agree. The prize recognises what has been demonstrated, and the redefinition of the second is a decision for metrologists. I would only add that the lack of a fundamental-constant result means the citation should speak of new possibilities and not of delivered discoveries.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators first as a new state of matter, but concedes that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and the 3D topological insulator work make the three-name attribution fragile, and names the lattice clock as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I understand why a new state of matter appeals to this committee, and I consider the interpretation of the HgTe edge conductance well established. I defer to him and to Johansson on condensed matter. His own account of the attribution is what holds me back. If Zhang's death leaves the proposal that identified HgTe unrecognisable, and the 3D work cannot fit under a three-person cap, then the committee would be making a choice that colleagues in the field might see as arbitrary. I do not want a prize whose credit is the first thing people argue about. If he can write a citation that stays with the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and is accepted as fair, I would take B048 seriously, and that is why I now list it as an alternative. But I would not rank it ahead of a result where the two names are agreed by all eight members, and where he himself calls the clock the cleaner choice.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase as the conceptual root of Chern numbers, quantum Hall physics and topological band programmes, and acknowledges that priority (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar, Simon), the death of Bohm and age all weigh against it.
responses.response: I read his argument again and I have more sympathy for it than my ranking suggests. As an atomic theorist I use the geometric phase regularly, for example in the phase of a photoelectron wave packet, and I like asking what a phase means. But the priority questions he names are the ones I cannot resolve from memory, and Bohm cannot be recognised. A prize that honours a foundational idea decades after others have been recognised for its consequences would also need a very clear sentence on who found it first. I have therefore moved B034 out of my alternatives and replaced it with B048, since the Kane-Mele line is the part of his chain of consequences where I think a recognition can be justified on experimental grounds. I would still like to hear how he would phrase the priority statement for Berry and Aharonov.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, records that he is in the B013 group, that he is not an atomic physicist, and that he relies on colleagues for the priority questions on B013. He ranks IceCube first and the lattice clock second.
responses.response: Since he has said that he relies on colleagues on this, I will say plainly what I can and cannot give him. I can say that the physical argument for the magic wavelength is sound and that the 10^-18 evaluations were reproduced by several laboratories. I cannot reliably say who among the many contributors made which lattice-clock proposal first, because I am recalling this and not checking documents. I therefore support his suggestion that an expert review of the priority record for the early lattice-clock proposals would be sensible before the final ballot. I would not let that review change the structure of the prize. I would only ask that it checks whether a third name is warranted. IceCube is not among my alternatives, but I do not oppose it, and I defer to his and Danielsson's field knowledge there, and my concern remains attribution in a large collaboration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a discovery or as outstanding measurement science, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes. A citation worded around the lattice principle helps, but cannot settle the question.

Whether Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg or others have claims that would make a two-name credit unfair. I cannot verify this from memory and would want an expert review of the early lattice-clock proposals.

Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second or for a first fundamental-physics result. I would accept a limit on a variation of constants or a dark-sector coupling as an adequate result, but I do not think the prize needs to wait for a detection.

Whether a second part, for example B001 on quantum simulation with ultracold atoms, would be stronger than the clock alone, and whether the right three names are Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger or Bloch, Greiner and Zoller. The tension between these experimental and theoretical claims is not resolved for me.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (Lund, 2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. None of the credited names on B013 (Katori, Ye) is a collaborator, and my profile documents no link with them, so I see no specific recusal issue. I work in theoretical atomic physics, which is close to this field, and I have said above that this may colour my judgment. I also have no personal link to any other part I list as an alternative, but I recall priority for B013 and B001 from memory and not from verified documents.
